title: Two Channels for One Head Turn

scenes.visual: Title card: Two Channels for One Head Turn.

scenes.tts: Every head movement has parts that last and parts that change fast. Your balance organs report both, on two kinds of nerve fibre. Regular afferents fire like a steady clock. They carry sustained motion in their firing rate. Irregular afferents fire unevenly. They carry rapid changes in the precise timing of their spikes. Two channels, one head turn. Together they feed the reflexes that keep your gaze and posture steady.

scenes.visual: A head turning once; its velocity trace splits into a blue fibre with evenly spaced ticks whose rate rises and falls smoothly, and a purple fibre with uneven ticks clustered tightly at the fast edges of the turn; both arrows end at eye and neck icons.

scenes.tts: Where does each channel come from? Recordings from single fibres, traced back with dye, built a map. Regular fibres mostly start in the outer zone, on type two hair cells with small bouton endings. Irregular fibres mostly start in the central zone, where flask-shaped type one cells sit inside a cup-shaped ending called a calyx. The map holds for populations, not for every fibre.

scenes.visual: Plan view of a sensory epithelium with a shaded central zone; a dye-filled fibre traced from each zone; zoom to a cylindrical type II cell with boutons (blue) and a flask-shaped type I cell in a calyx (purple); a small caption chip: populations, not rules.

scenes.tts: The calyx is built for speed. Both hair cell types release glutamate from vesicles. Yet a mature mouse type one cell still made its calyx fire when either of two proteins needed for vesicle release was missing. Recordings in turtles, a different animal, point to a possible route. Current and potassium cross the narrow cleft directly, with no vesicles and no gap junctions. This non-quantal transmission has little synaptic delay.

scenes.visual: Both cells shown with ribbon vesicles; vesicles dim on the type I cell yet the calyx still spikes; two pipettes on one hair cell and calyx pair; a fast arrow and a slower potassium cloud crossing the cleft, both double-headed.

scenes.tts: Reviews propose that this short delay serves the fast reflexes. The channels form as the ear matures. In young mice, new potassium channels speed up hair cell signals, make type one transmission non-quantal, and make afferent firing more irregular. Clinicians use the fast channel too: sound and vibration tests of balance mostly drive the irregular fibres.

scenes.visual: A timeline from young to mature mouse: potassium channels appear in the membrane, the receptor potential steepens, the calyx arrow becomes the fast route, the fibre's ticks become uneven; then a vibrating bone conductor lighting only the purple fibres.

scenes.tts: Afferents fire whether you turn your head or something turns it for you. In alert monkeys, Roy and Cullen found vestibular-only neurons that responded much less to the monkey's own turns. That cancelling held only when neck feedback matched what the motor command predicted. When the match failed, the response came back.

scenes.visual: Reuse the existing active versus passive heads and the match box: afferent ticks run under both turns; a central neuron's response is tall for the passive turn and small for the active turn with matching neck feedback; a red mismatch restores the tall response.

scenes.tts: Keep three ideas in order. The ear splits head motion into a sustained channel and a fast channel. The calyx can drive its fibre without vesicles, which is thought to keep the fast channel fast. And in the vestibular-only neurons tested, the cancelling is central, and it held only when neck feedback matched the prediction. You still feel your own turns; what changes is the reflex that would fight them.
